performers: The Tudor Consort; Michael Stewart, director
intro: Palestrina’s five-voice motet Sicut lilium inter spinas sets the image of a lily among thorns in long, overlapping phrases, with two tenor parts in the middle of the texture. The Tudor Consort sings.

sections.label: A · Lily among thorns, imitative entries
sections.mNote: The upper voice begins; four other voices take up its phrase.

sections.label: B · My beloved among the daughters
sections.mNote: Inner voices enter while the upper voice holds its note.

sections.label: C · Alleluia passes through the choir
sections.mNote: Overlapping Alleluias lead to the five-part close.

cues.title: Opening entries, five voices
cues.text: The highest voice begins alone. The alto takes up its phrase, then the tenor; the bass and second tenor enter later. Each voice begins “Sicut lilium” while another is still singing the line.
cues.evidence: Palestrina’s Werke, volume I, edited by Theodor de Witt (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1862), No. 21, pp. 90–91: the five opening entries. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f5/IMSLP55722-PMLP115176-Tomus_I.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First book of motets, Rome, 1569
cues.text: This five-voice motet comes from Palestrina’s first book of motets for five, six and seven voices, printed in Rome in 1569. John Milsom suggested from its style that it may be a student work, though he found in it “all the poise and polish” for which Palestrina’s music is famous.
cues.evidence: Title page of the 1569 print (Rome, heirs of Valerio and Aloisio Dorico), reproduced at the head of Palestrina’s Werke, vol. I (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1862): Liber primus … Motettorum quae partim quinis, partim senis, partim septenis vocibus concinantur; this motet is No. 21 there. John Milsom on this five-voice Sicut lilium, the source of “poise and polish” and of the student-work suggestion: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W15060_GBLLH1645012 . Peter Phillips confirms that the Mass Sicut lilium is based on the motet from the First Book of Motets of 1569, and the Tudor Consort album pairs the motet with that Mass: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W15061_810202

cues.title: Text from the Song of Songs
cues.text: The words “Sicut lilium inter spinas” (“As a lily among thorns”) come from the Song of Songs. In the text, the beloved stands among the daughters of Adam as the flower stands among thorns.
cues.evidence: The Latin text appears in the 1862 score, No. 21, pp. 90–93. John Milsom identifies its Song of Songs source in his programme note: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W15060_GBLLH1645012 . Translation ours.

cues.title: Alto and tenor, “sic amica mea”
cues.text: The alto and tenor sing the next words, “sic amica mea” — “so is my beloved”. Above them, the highest voice holds the end of its earlier phrase, so that for a while the choir sings both halves of the comparison at once.
cues.evidence: Palestrina’s Werke, volume I (1862), No. 21, p. 91, bottom system: altus and tenor begin sic amica mea beneath the cantus’s sustained spinas. Translation ours; the section boundary locates the passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Parody Mass on the motet
cues.text: Palestrina used this motet again in his Missa Sicut lilium inter spinas. The opening phrase of the motet becomes the beginning of the Kyrie, with the five voices now setting the words of the Mass.
cues.evidence: Peter Phillips describes the motet’s opening imitations and their transfer to the first Kyrie: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W15061_810202 .

cues.title: Closing Alleluia
cues.text: The closing Alleluia begins in the tenor and passes through the choir, with short running notes set against long held ones. The voices end at different times. The tenor reaches its last note while the other parts are still singing.
cues.evidence: Palestrina’s Werke, volume I (1862), No. 21, pp. 93–94: tenor begins Alleluia; the final system holds the tenor’s last note beneath the continuing parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: New words beneath a held note
transitions.from: A · Lily among thorns, imitative entries
transitions.to: B · My beloved among the daughters
transitions.how: The cantus holds the last syllable of spinas. Beneath it, the alto and tenor begin sic amica mea. The second tenor follows, and the bass enters again after a rest.
transitions.evidence: Palestrina’s Werke, volume I, edited by Theodor de Witt (1862), No. 21, p. 91, bottom system.

transitions.title: The tenor begins Alleluia
transitions.from: B · My beloved among the daughters
transitions.to: C · Alleluia passes through the choir
transitions.how: The tenor begins Alleluia while the bass is still holding the end of Adae. The second tenor enters next, then the alto and the highest voice. The word passes from part to part in shorter notes, and the bass enters last.
transitions.evidence: Palestrina’s Werke, volume I (1862), No. 21, p. 93, middle system, continuing to p. 94.

source.title: Palestrina, Motettorum, Liber 1, No. 21, ed. Theodor de Witt (1862)
source.locator: Printed pp. 90–94 (PDF pp. 104–108). Five unaccompanied parts: cantus, altus, tenor, quintus (second tenor) and bassus.

timeline.note: The highest voice begins alone; alto, tenor, bass and second tenor take up its phrase.

fields.note: These are credits for the nominated recording, not the separate Hyperion performances consulted for programme notes. Individual singers and choir size are not identified.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Unaccompanied motet for cantus, altus, tenor, second tenor and bassus
fields.note: The five-part score is the motet, not the Mass of the same name. The album lists the motet as track 1 and the Mass movements separately. The choir’s exact performing edition and pitch are not identified.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: FMA describes a live minidisc recording and gives the album date as 29 July 2007. The choir’s own archive documents the matching Renaissance Influences programme on that date. Their conjunction supports a probable session date, but the track description does not explicitly identify the session day. The FMA track’s 20 August 2010 is its online release.

fields.label: Place

fields.note: The official archive supplies the venue for the matching 29 July 2007 concert. The link between that concert and the recording is inferred from title, director, programme and album date, not stated in the track description.
